WENTWORTH GANGSTERS commissioned

By: Julie Laurenz | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Wentworth, in Durban, is engulfed in a wave of violent drug gang warfare, with 3 gunned down over Christmas. Desperate the community plan to confront the gangster kingpins.

Summary:
The Durban south basin suburb has in the past been associated with toxic spills and air pollution emanating from refineries in the area. But in the past two years gang warfare has erupted in Wentworth, with three people wounded and a young football star dead on Christmas day.
The war is being fueled by drugs and the community is living in fear.

Senior police (they won’t talk on camera – but I might be able to convince one to do a hidden ID?) and community leaders believe local police are not equipped to deal with this violent crime.


Further information:
TRAGIC CHRISTMAS DAY DRIVE BY SHOOTING
Instead of celebrating the New Year, a Wentworth family will bury a loved one who was killed in a drive-by shooting near their home. 22 year old Tremaine Marais was in the wrong place at the wrong time.
The young local football star had only just appeared in the Daily News for helping his team, the Merewent Suburb Football Club win 4 trophies last in 2014. He’d joined the club when he was 9 and had climbed through the ranks.
The Hawks are investigating the crime, who closed part of the road where the shooting began, to reconstruct the crime scene and speak to potential witnesses and residents. With the aid of a metal detector, investigators found five bullets and cartridge cases.
Children from the neighbouring flats also handed over shell casings they had found on the road.
Police are trying to piece together the sequence of events, based on witness accounts.
It is alleged that men in a white bakkie began shooting at a group of people standing near the flats in Wiest Road.
It is alleged Tremaine had walked into the shooting incident and, when he turned to run, he was shot in the back. His body was found by a passerby about a kilometre from the shooting. Stray bullets also hit buildings and a parked car.
Agnes Marais said her son’s body was still warm when she arrived at the scene. “My child worked hard to earn a living and was killed in the prime of his life.”
Earlier this month KZN MEC for Transport, Community Safety and Liaison, Willies Mchunu, met the residents of Wentworth and declared war on gangsterism in the suburb, urging the community to mobilise against criminality in the area.
HISTORY REPEATS
Leroy Johnson, 19, was found guilty last month of stabbing his friend, Kerwin Abrahams, 22, of Wentworth, killing him, on Christmas Eve 2011.
He stabbed Abrahams in the heart with a knife he carried to protect himself against gangsters in Wentworth.
OTHER GANG MURDERS:
22 Dec 2014. Two men were arrested a street away. They were charged with the attempted murder of three people in the street.
14 November: A vendor selling mangoes in Merebank was shot and then driven over when a gang fight spilled into the street where she was trading. Nonhlanhla Ngwekazi, 49, survived.
4 November: Tyrell Watson, 24, was driving his father’s bakkie when gunmen sprayed the vehicle with bullets. While the vehicle was on its roof, a gunman approached and shot Watson in the head.
There were another 5 gang related shootings in just two weeks earlier on in 2014.
Community activist Desmond D’Sa says the community are afraid that this could become a full-on turf war and Wentworth could become ungovernable, like the Cape Flats, if the problem isn’t contained.
UNDERWORLD KINGPIN:
Police have linked the recent shootings to the return of an underworld kingpin. He was making a big push to control the drug trade in the area, so more shootings could be expected.
The gangs are known to sell drugs such as cocaine, heroin, mandrax, rocks (crack cocaine), dagga and, more recently, whoonga, a popular drug in the community.
The community have been pleading for a specialised police unit to be set up to deal with the problem. Desmond: “There are a lot of good cops in Wentworth, but their hard work is being undone by a small element working with the gangs. That’s why we need a specialised unit from outside Wentworth to deal with this problem. The killing of young men in our community has to stop,” he said.
THE GANGS
The Destroyers and G-Section are the dominant gangs. Their strongholds, three-storey blocks of flats, are 500m apart.
FOOTAGE OF THE GANG STRONGHOLDS
I have a local PI who says he can get footage of the strongholds.
COMMUNITY PROTEST
The strife-torn community are planning to “confront the gangs”. They are holding a “healing walk” next weekend. 12 church communities and worshippers from the local mosque will walk through the suburb. They will visit at least 10 drug hot spots where they plan to speak to drug users and peddlers in the hope of getting them to change.
Pastor Earl Wilkinson, 58, from First Dominion Ministries, and a resident of Wentworth for 54 years said: “Wentworth is sick and needs healing.”
Wentworth suffers from overcrowding, unemployment and a mix of overflowing anger and apathy.
“Three to four generations stay in one flat... and right now we are sitting on powder keg.”
Wilkinson is a part of Operation Sukuma Sakhe (which means stand up and let’s build), which aims to fight the drug scourge.
“The community struggles with the perception that drug dealers and the SAPS are in collusion and people are scared to go to the SAPS... The reality is that it is a community that has been marginalised and has poor service delivery,” he said.

Press Release:


Wentworth Drugs
Buildings pockmarked with bullet holes are home to innocent people who live in constant fear that each new day could herald more casualties of the gang war raging in Wentworth, Durban. Carte Blanche’s cameras go into the heart of this gangland to meet the bereaved mothers and fathers taking on the rot.



Script:


WENTWORTH GANGS EDIT SCRIPT

Life in Wentworth, Durban is tough. For decades residents have battled air pollution and toxic
spills emanating from refineries and factories in the area.

Now they are caught up in another war. A growing epidemic of drug usage and gangs is tearing this community apart.

Metro Police regularly raid the area, enforcing bylaws and looking for stolen vehicles. We went with them on one of their operations.

LINK:
We are arriving in Wentworth. The flats that we are passing by is understood to be
the area where the drug activity and the gangster-ism takes place. And it’s in the heart of this
area where we are going to go tonight.

People moved to these flats in the 1950’s after being forcibly removed from elsewhere under apartheid’s group areas act. Today the buildings are overcrowded with as many as four generations sharing a two bedroom apartment.

Most of the residents, didn’t want to talk about the gangs.

Resident:
People are scared. What’s going to happen when I’m finished speaking here? What’s going to happen to me around the corner?

These youngsters said they belong to a gang and showed us walls pockmarked with bullet holes.

Bongani: So who made these bullet marks here?
Resident: Those people from the top there
Bongani: Who are those people there?
Resident: Gangsters!
Resident: They are our rival gang – they hate us and we hate them.

The community are worried about an all out turf war.4 people were caught up in shootings on Christmas day.

Agnes Marais 22 year old son, Tramaine, was one of those gunned down – caught in the middle of an alleged drive by shooting.

He’d tried to run but was shot in the back and killed. His body was still warm when she got to the crime scene.

Agnes:
I remember saying, “It’s my son, and I need to pray for my child”. And they allowed me to go to the body and I lay my hands on him and I prayed for him”

Agnes says her son was not part of a gang. When other young boys were being draw into a life of crime, Tramaine joined a local soccer club instead.

He scored 10 winning goals for his team last year, and was one of the lucky few who had a job.


Wentworth may be one of Durban’s’ most industrialised areas, yet unemployment sits at around 40%.

Bongani: What does the loss of Tremaine mean to you?

Agnes:
Everything. Loosing Tremaine is losing someone that lifts me up. Someone who took care of me and my husband. His father is going to have to do it on his own.

Desmond D’Sa is a community activist, and says it’s not the first time he’s come up against gangs in Wentworth.

In the 80’s he and the residents drove emerging gangs out of the area , by building sports clubs to
Entertain the youth. But the playgrounds and parks are rundown now.

Desmond: Since 1984 we never had a coat of paint from the present government, despite the fact that we paying our rent an’all.

Bongani: It’s the whole broken window thing, isn’t it?
Desmond: It’s the whole broken window thing Ja.

“Broken Window syndrome” is a theory in criminology, where people stop caring about things like trash and blight. Apathy becomes the norm, and crime creeps into the area.

He says the new generation gangs, terrorising the neighbourhood , are vicious – fuelled by greed
and spurred on by drug lords who have moved into the area.

Desmond:
The lucrative drug trade is driving gang bosses to use the youngsters and the youth in particular to fight for, to fight to control the trade and to eliminate the opponents.

In July last year a teenager was mowed down, allegedly with an automatic machine gun in the stairwell of one of the blocks.

And in November another youngster was shot execution style after being run off
the road by the gunmen.

Devin Loggenberg was also shot on Christmas day. But unlike Tramaine – he is a gangster.

The bullet lodged in his back and he is temporarily paralysed from the waist down.

UPSOUND: Hi Devin, Bongani.....

Devin joined a gang known as the “Hime Street Flat Cats “or HFC when he was 15. He says he was shot because he tried to leave the gang.

Bongani:
I heard that if you grow up there it’s hard to not be in a gang?
Devin:
That’s the thing now. These guys want to be in a gang now, just for name. You
have to be strong, you can’t show weakness.

It’s also a way for many of these young men to make money.

Devin:
Easy money to be made.

Desmond:
The talk amongst the gangs is that certain gang leaders are making over R100,000 a day.
Particularly on the weekend, Friday, Saturday and Sundays the sales are at its highest. The drugs
are sold like sweets out of a shop – a tuck shop.

We filmed this footage during a stakeout, overlooking the “HFC “gang’s turf.

Over a 2hour period we watched car after car arrive out front. The occupants would then walk
through to the court yard at the back where the appeared to be buying drugs ....

....which they either consumed on the premises...

...or stashed away for later.

One buyer seemed to wrap his in a piece of plastic trash and hide in his bonnet before driving off.

Bongani: They also sell them to the school kids, don’t they?
Devin: Ja, definitely....definitely.

In November 2013 a 15 year old pupil was allegedly stabbed to death at a Wentworth school in
gang related violence.

Devin says it’s dangerous for drug users to swap suppliers. The gangs demand loyalty from both member s and clients.

The Flats fill an area of about 3km square, so most of the gang strongholds are no more than 500m apart.

LINK: The rivalry could be between that building and the one opposite it.

Devin:
There is a crew on this corner and a crew on the next corner. Serving your
own customers and serving your own customers.

And suspicions run high.

An informant, with close ties to a gang called the “G-Section”, wore a hidden camera and pretended he wanted to buy drugs from “The Destroyers” – a rival gang.

Gang member: You P*ss. One of these days you gonna get f*%ked up. I’m not gonna serve you, I’m gonna f*%k you up.
Informant: Sorry.

Desmond:
They sell openly, plainly without fear of being arrested by the police.

During the HFC stakeout, this South African Police Services van drove into the gangs compound. None of the alleged gang members seemed perturbed by their presence.

Possibly because the SAPS deny there is a gang problem in Wentworth.

Brigadier James Sayer is the cluster commander for the area.

Bongani: So, as far as the police are concerned there is no gangster-ism in Wentworth?
Sayer: No, there are no gangster-ism in Wentworth.

They say these are just informal groups who happen to commit crime.

Sayer: It’s not dealt with in the same way that you have to deal with formal gangs in other areas.

He’s talking about highly organised gangs like the 26’s and 28’s on the cape Flats.

Bongani: What are the gang names?
Ganster: WDS, the Destroyers
Bongani: The Destroyers.

Bongani: So the Fat Cats and the Destroyers and HFC, what do those
names mean to you?
Sayer: Nothing, nothing.

Desperate the community held a march last Saturday to draw attention to their plight. Elizabeth
Bower’s son was allegedly stabbed and killed by gangster s on New Year’s day 2014.

Bongani: As a mother who has lost a child in this way what do say when the police say “ There are no gangs in Wentworth”?
Elizabeth: No – that’s a lie


Bongani: But Brigadier, with respect, you know, the chances of people being shot in drive
by shootings. On Christmas Day there were at least four shootings, that’s not general
crime.
Sayer: The drive-by shooting you are referring to that matter is being investigated by the Hawks.

Brigadier Sayer is talking about Tremaine’s case. So far there have been no arrests.

Sayer: Other incidents if we go and analyse them that happened in the Hime Street area could be seen as part of the Christmas festivities.

He’s referring to Devin.

We visited “Hime Street”, home of the HFC’s during the metro police raid.

LINK: Hime Street is also called “Crime Street” because this is where most of the gang related crime takes place.

It’s also where we did our stake out. Although we found no signs of drug dealing - this man was arrested for assaulting an officer.

The Metro police say they do not have a mandate to contradict the SAPS stand that there are no gangs in Wentworth. They will however continue to do regular patrols.

Desmond says it’s up to the residents now to prove Brigadier Sayer wrong. He’s called on the community to come forward with information, despite the dangers.!

Desmond UPSOUND: We cannot complain if we don’t provide the information!
Desmond: In the past when the community gave the information the Wentworth Police they had their homes petrol bombed.

4 flats, including Desmond’s have been set ablaze.

Undeterred, he’s finding ways to help the community give tips anonymously. Some of the churches encourage their parish members to slip information into the collection boxes. They are also working with government to get the flats refurbished.

Elizabeth: Blood is being shed all the time, drugs are going in and out – guns in and out . So what are CUT. So I think we need help. I dunno how we are going to get help...But someone needs to come and do something about it.

Carte Blanche’s cameras go into the heart of this gangland to meet the bereaved mothers and fathers taking on the rot. Script: WENTWORTH GANGS EDIT SCRIPT Life in Wentworth, Durban is tough. For decades residents have battled air pollution and toxic spills emanating from refineries and factories in the area. Now they are caught up in another war. A growing epidemic of drug usage and gangs is tearing this community apart. Metro Police regularly raid the area, enforcing bylaws and looking for stolen vehicles. We went with them on one of their operations. LINK: We are arriving in Wentworth. The flats that we are passing by is understood to be the area where the drug activity and the gangster-ism takes place. And it’s in the heart of this area where we are going to go tonight. People moved to these flats in the 1950’s after being forcibly removed from elsewhere under apartheid’s group areas act. Today the buildings are overcrowded with as many as four generations sharing a two bedroom apartment. Most of the residents, didn’t want to talk about the gangs. Resident: People are scared. What’s going to happen when I’m finished speaking here? What’s going to happen to me around the corner? These youngsters said they belong to a gang and showed us walls pockmarked with bullet holes. Bongani: So who made these bullet marks here? Resident: Those people from the top there Bongani: Who are those people there? Resident: Gangsters! Resident: They are our rival gang – they hate us and we hate them. The community are worried about an all out turf war.4 people were caught up in shootings on Christmas day. Agnes Marais 22 year old son, Tramaine, was one of those gunned down – caught in the middle of an alleged drive by shooting. He’d tried to run but was shot in the back and killed. His body was still warm when she got to the crime scene. Agnes: I remember saying, “It’s my son, and I need to pray for my child”. And they allowed me to go to the body and I lay my hands on him and I prayed for him” Agnes says her son was not part of a gang. When other young boys were being draw into a life of crime, Tramaine joined a local soccer club instead. He scored 10 winning goals for his team last year, and was one of the lucky few who had a job. Wentworth may be one of Durban’s’ most industrialised areas, yet unemployment sits at around 40%. Bongani: What does the loss of Tremaine mean to you? Agnes: Everything. Loosing Tremaine is losing someone that lifts me up. Someone who took care of me and my husband. His father is going to have to do it on his own. Desmond D’Sa is a community activist, and says it’s not the first time he’s come up against gangs in Wentworth. In the 80’s he and the residents drove emerging gangs out of the area , by building sports clubs to Entertain the youth. But the playgrounds and parks are rundown now. Desmond: Since 1984 we never had a coat of paint from the present government, despite the fact that we paying our rent an’all. Bongani: It’s the whole broken window thing, isn’t it? Desmond: It’s the whole broken window thing Ja. “Broken Window syndrome” is a theory in criminology, where people stop caring about things like trash and blight. Apathy becomes the norm, and crime creeps into the area. He says the new generation gangs, terrorising the neighbourhood , are vicious – fuelled by greed and spurred on by drug lords who have moved into the area. Desmond: The lucrative drug trade is driving gang bosses to use the youngsters and the youth in particular to fight for, to fight to control the trade and to eliminate the opponents. In July last year a teenager was mowed down, allegedly with an automatic machine gun in the stairwell of one of the blocks. And in November another youngster was shot execution style after being run off the road by the gunmen. Devin Loggenberg was also shot on Christmas day. But unlike Tramaine – he is a gangster. The bullet lodged in his back and he is temporarily paralysed from the waist down. UPSOUND: Hi Devin, Bongani..... Devin joined a gang known as the “Hime Street Flat Cats “or HFC when he was 15. He says he was shot because he tried to leave the gang. Bongani: I heard that if you grow up there it’s hard to not be in a gang? Devin: That’s the thing now. These guys want to be in a gang now, just for name. You have to be strong, you can’t show weakness. It’s also a way for many of these young men to make money. Devin: Easy money to be made. Desmond: The talk amongst the gangs is that certain gang leaders are making over R100,000 a day. Particularly on the weekend, Friday, Saturday and Sundays the sales are at its highest. The drugs are sold like sweets out of a shop – a tuck shop. We filmed this footage during a stakeout, overlooking the “HFC “gang’s turf. Over a 2hour period we watched car after car arrive out front. The occupants would then walk through to the court yard at the back where the appeared to be buying drugs .... ....which they either consumed on the premises... ...or stashed away for later. One buyer seemed to wrap his in a piece of plastic trash and hide in his bonnet before driving off. Bongani: They also sell them to the school kids, don’t they? Devin: Ja, definitely....definitely. In November 2013 a 15 year old pupil was allegedly stabbed to death at a Wentworth school in gang related violence. Devin says it’s dangerous for drug users to swap suppliers. The gangs demand loyalty from both member s and clients. The Flats fill an area of about 3km square, so most of the gang strongholds are no more than 500m apart. LINK: The rivalry could be between that building and the one opposite it. Devin: There is a crew on this corner and a crew on the next corner. Serving your own customers and serving your own customers. And suspicions run high. An informant, with close ties to a gang called the “G-Section”, wore a hidden camera and pretended he wanted to buy drugs from “The Destroyers” – a rival gang. Gang member: You P*ss. One of these days you gonna get f*%ked up. I’m not gonna serve you, I’m gonna f*%k you up. Informant: Sorry. Desmond: They sell openly, plainly without fear of being arrested by the police. During the HFC stakeout, this South African Police Services van drove into the gangs compound. None of the alleged gang members seemed perturbed by their presence. Possibly because the SAPS deny there is a gang problem in Wentworth. Brigadier James Sayer is the cluster commander for the area. Bongani: So, as far as the police are concerned there is no gangster-ism in Wentworth? Sayer: No, there are no gangster-ism in Wentworth. They say these are just informal groups who happen to commit crime. Sayer: It’s not dealt with in the same way that you have to deal with formal gangs in other areas. He’s talking about highly organised gangs like the 26’s and 28’s on the cape Flats. Bongani: What are the gang names? Ganster: WDS, the Destroyers Bongani: The Destroyers. Bongani: So the Fat Cats and the Destroyers and HFC, what do those names mean to you? Sayer: Nothing, nothing. Desperate the community held a march last Saturday to draw attention to their plight. Elizabeth Bower’s son was allegedly stabbed and killed by gangster s on New Year’s day 2014. Bongani: As a mother who has lost a child in this way what do say when the police say “ There are no gangs in Wentworth”? Elizabeth: No – that’s a lie Bongani: But Brigadier, with respect, you know, the chances of people being shot in drive by shootings. On Christmas Day there were at least four shootings, that’s not general crime. Sayer: The drive-by shooting you are referring to that matter is being investigated by the Hawks. Brigadier Sayer is talking about Tremaine’s case. So far there have been no arrests. Sayer: Other incidents if we go and analyse them that happened in the Hime Street area could be seen as part of the Christmas festivities. He’s referring to Devin. We visited “Hime Street”, home of the HFC’s during the metro police raid. LINK: Hime Street is also called “Crime Street” because this is where most of the gang related crime takes place. It’s also where we did our stake out. Although we found no signs of drug dealing - this man was arrested for assaulting an officer. The Metro police say they do not have a mandate to contradict the SAPS stand that there are no gangs in Wentworth. They will however continue to do regular patrols. Desmond says it’s up to the residents now to prove Brigadier Sayer wrong. He’s called on the community to come forward with information, despite the dangers.! Desmond UPSOUND: We cannot complain if we don’t provide the information! Desmond: In the past when the community gave the information the Wentworth Police they had their homes petrol bombed. 4 flats, including Desmond’s have been set ablaze. Undeterred, he’s finding ways to help the community give tips anonymously. Some of the churches encourage their parish members to slip information into the collection boxes. They are also working with government to get the flats refurbished. Elizabeth: Blood is being shed all the time, drugs are going in and out – guns in and out . So what are CUT. So I think we need help. I dunno how we are going to get help...But someone needs to come and do something about it. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Wentworth, in Durban, is engulfed in a wave of violent drug gang warfare, with 3 gunned down over Christmas. Desperate the community plan to confront the gangster kingpins.
metadata.Summary: The Durban south basin suburb has in the past been associated with toxic spills and air pollution emanating from refineries in the area. But in the past two years gang warfare has erupted in Wentworth, with three people wounded and a young football star dead on Christmas day. The war is being fueled by drugs and the community is living in fear. Senior police (they won’t talk on camera – but I might be able to convince one to do a hidden ID?) and community leaders believe local police are not equipped to deal with this violent crime.
metadata.Further information: TRAGIC CHRISTMAS DAY DRIVE BY SHOOTING Instead of celebrating the New Year, a Wentworth family will bury a loved one who was killed in a drive-by shooting near their home. 22 year old Tremaine Marais was in the wrong place at the wrong time. The young local football star had only just appeared in the Daily News for helping his team, the Merewent Suburb Football Club win 4 trophies last in 2014. He’d joined the club when he was 9 and had climbed through the ranks. The Hawks are investigating the crime, who closed part of the road where the shooting began, to reconstruct the crime scene and speak to potential witnesses and residents. With the aid of a metal detector, investigators found five bullets and cartridge cases. Children from the neighbouring flats also handed over shell casings they had found on the road. Police are trying to piece together the sequence of events, based on witness accounts. It is alleged that men in a white bakkie began shooting at a group of people standing near the flats in Wiest Road. It is alleged Tremaine had walked into the shooting incident and, when he turned to run, he was shot in the back. His body was found by a passerby about a kilometre from the shooting. Stray bullets also hit buildings and a parked car. Agnes Marais said her son’s body was still warm when she arrived at the scene. “My child worked hard to earn a living and was killed in the prime of his life.” Earlier this month KZN MEC for Transport, Community Safety and Liaison, Willies Mchunu, met the residents of Wentworth and declared war on gangsterism in the suburb, urging the community to mobilise against criminality in the area. HISTORY REPEATS Leroy Johnson, 19, was found guilty last month of stabbing his friend, Kerwin Abrahams, 22, of Wentworth, killing him, on Christmas Eve 2011. He stabbed Abrahams in the heart with a knife he carried to protect himself against gangsters in Wentworth. OTHER GANG MURDERS: 22 Dec 2014. Two men were arrested a street away. They were charged with the attempted murder of three people in the street. 14 November: A vendor selling mangoes in Merebank was shot and then driven over when a gang fight spilled into the street where she was trading. Nonhlanhla Ngwekazi, 49, survived. 4 November: Tyrell Watson, 24, was driving his father’s bakkie when gunmen sprayed the vehicle with bullets. While the vehicle was on its roof, a gunman approached and shot Watson in the head. There were another 5 gang related shootings in just two weeks earlier on in 2014. Community activist Desmond D’Sa says the community are afraid that this could become a full-on turf war and Wentworth could become ungovernable, like the Cape Flats, if the problem isn’t contained. UNDERWORLD KINGPIN: Police have linked the recent shootings to the return of an underworld kingpin. He was making a big push to control the drug trade in the area, so more shootings could be expected. The gangs are known to sell drugs such as cocaine, heroin, mandrax, rocks (crack cocaine), dagga and, more recently, whoonga, a popular drug in the community. The community have been pleading for a specialised police unit to be set up to deal with the problem. Desmond: “There are a lot of good cops in Wentworth, but their hard work is being undone by a small element working with the gangs. That’s why we need a specialised unit from outside Wentworth to deal with this problem. The killing of young men in our community has to stop,” he said. THE GANGS The Destroyers and G-Section are the dominant gangs. Their strongholds, three-storey blocks of flats, are 500m apart. FOOTAGE OF THE GANG STRONGHOLDS I have a local PI who says he can get footage of the strongholds. COMMUNITY PROTEST The strife-torn community are planning to “confront the gangs”. They are holding a “healing walk” next weekend. 12 church communities and worshippers from the local mosque will walk through the suburb. They will visit at least 10 drug hot spots where they plan to speak to drug users and peddlers in the hope of getting them to change. Pastor Earl Wilkinson, 58, from First Dominion Ministries, and a resident of Wentworth for 54 years said: “Wentworth is sick and needs healing.” Wentworth suffers from overcrowding, unemployment and a mix of overflowing anger and apathy. “Three to four generations stay in one flat... and right now we are sitting on powder keg.” Wilkinson is a part of Operation Sukuma Sakhe (which means stand up and let’s build), which aims to fight the drug scourge. “The community struggles with the perception that drug dealers and the SAPS are in collusion and people are scared to go to the SAPS... The reality is that it is a community that has been marginalised and has poor service delivery,” he said.
